title: Database Design Revision Notes: ER Modeling, Keys and Normalization
summary: Quick revision of ER modeling (entities, attributes, relationships, cardinality), the key hierarchy, functional dependencies, normal forms 1NF to BCNF, and the anomalies they prevent.

chapters.title: ER Model Mental Model
points: Entity = a thing you store facts about (Student); entity set = all such things; drawn as a rectangle, rows in a table
Attribute types: simple vs composite (name → first/last), single-valued vs multivalued (phones), derived (age from dob), stored vs derived
Weak entity: no key of its own, depends on an owner entity via identifying relationship, key = owner key + partial key (Dependent of Employee)
Relationship = association between entities (Student enrolls in Course); relationships can carry attributes (grade on enrolls)
ER to tables: entity → table, multivalued attribute → separate table, M:N relationship → junction table with both foreign keys

chapters.title: Cardinality and Participation
points: Cardinality ratios: 1:1, 1:N, M:N; 1:N puts the FK on the N side (Order.customer_id)
M:N always needs a junction table; its PK is usually the pair of FKs (student_id, course_id)
1:1 puts the FK on either side, with a UNIQUE constraint on it; prefer the side with total participation
Total participation (double line, every instance must take part, NOT NULL FK) vs partial participation (optional, nullable FK)
Common mistake: storing an M:N relationship as a comma-separated list column or putting the FK on the 1 side

chapters.title: Keys: Super, Candidate, Primary, Foreign
points: Super key = any attribute set that uniquely identifies a row; supersets of a key are also super keys, e.g. {id}, {id, name}
Candidate key = minimal super key (no attribute can be removed); a table can have several; prime attributes belong to some candidate key
Primary key = the one chosen candidate key; unique and NOT NULL; at most one per table. Alternate keys = remaining candidates (UNIQUE)
Foreign key = column referencing another table's candidate/primary key; may be NULL and duplicated; ON DELETE CASCADE / SET NULL / RESTRICT decide child behavior
Hierarchy: super keys ⊇ candidate keys ⊇ primary key; composite key = key made of 2+ attributes; surrogate key = generated id with no business meaning

chapters.title: Functional Dependencies and Closure
points: X → Y means any two rows with equal X must have equal Y; it is a rule about the schema, not about the current data
Armstrong's axioms: reflexivity (Y ⊆ X ⇒ X → Y), augmentation (X → Y ⇒ XZ → YZ), transitivity (X → Y, Y → Z ⇒ X → Z)
Derived rules: union (X→Y, X→Z ⇒ X→YZ), decomposition (X→YZ ⇒ X→Y and X→Z)
Attribute closure X⁺: start with X, repeatedly add RHS of any FD whose LHS is inside the set; X is a super key iff X⁺ = all attributes
Find candidate keys: attributes never on any RHS must be in every key; test them with closure, then add attributes only as needed
Partial dependency = non-prime attribute depends on part of a composite key; transitive dependency = non-prime → non-prime via X → Y → Z

chapters.title: Normal Forms and Anomalies
points: Anomalies in one wide table: insert (can't add a course without a student), update (change a value in many rows and miss some), delete (removing the last student loses the course)
1NF: atomic values only, no repeating groups or multivalued cells, each row identifiable by a key
2NF: 1NF + no partial dependency (every non-prime attribute depends on the whole candidate key); only matters for composite keys
3NF: 2NF + no transitive dependency; for every FD X→Y, X is a super key or Y is prime
BCNF: for every nontrivial FD X→Y, X must be a super key; stricter than 3NF, it can lose dependency preservation
Decompose by lifting the offending FD into its own table (X, Y); the split must be lossless-join, and normalizing too far costs joins, so denormalize on purpose for reads

chapters.title: Normalization Cheat Sheet
points: Key ladder: super key ⊇ candidate key ⊇ primary key; FK points at a key and may be NULL
Cardinality to tables: 1:N → FK on the N side; M:N → junction table; 1:1 → FK plus UNIQUE
Closure test: X is a super key iff X⁺ contains every attribute
Normal form tests: 1NF atomic; 2NF no partial dependency; 3NF no transitive dependency; BCNF every determinant is a super key
Memory line: every non-key attribute depends on the key (1NF), the whole key (2NF), and nothing but the key (3NF/BCNF)
